# Create new PDF from template with PHP

Working with PDF templates in PHP is a common requirement when you need to generate documents based on a pre-designed layout. You might have a DOCX file that has been converted to PDF, containing specific formatting, headers, and footers. The goal is often to take this static template and dynamically inject user dataâreplacing custom tags like `{name}` or `{invoice_number}` without recreating the entire document from scratch.

Many developers encounter a wall of libraries when searching for a solution. You will see mentions of FPDF, TCPDF, domPDF, and FPDI. While these tools are powerful, they often require manual positioning for every element. If you want to add text at specific coordinates or handle complex formatting, you must specify x, y positions, font families, sizes, and styles explicitly. This approach is essentially building the document from the ground up, which contradicts the need for a template-driven workflow.

The core challenge lies in finding a library that supports "search-and-replace" operations on an existing PDF stream without rendering it into a blank canvas first. Most standard libraries treat the PDF as a series of drawing commands rather than a layout file. FPDI (Free PDF Document Importer) comes closest to this capability by allowing you to import pages from an existing PDF and draw over them. However, even with FPDI, managing form fields or complex layouts often requires deep knowledge of the PDF structure.

If your requirement includes custom headers and footers that must remain consistent across all generated documents, a library that supports importing entire pages is essential. You need to load the template, iterate through specific markers (like `{customer_name}`), and replace them with actual data from a database. Additionally, you may need to append images or tables while preserving the original design integrity.

When evaluating options for shared hosting environments, memory consumption and dependency requirements become critical factors. Libraries that rely on heavy external dependencies or require extensive system libraries might fail silently on restricted servers. You also need flexibility in output: whether the final PDF is saved to disk, attached directly to an email via PHPMailer, or streamed to a browser download.

There is no single "Excel for PDF" library that offers a plug-and-play template engine out of the box like PHPExcel did for spreadsheets. The ecosystem leans heavily toward either full control (building from scratch) or limited templating capabilities. For those needing a robust solution, FPDI remains one of the few viable paths to truly load and manipulate an existing PDF layout in PHP, provided you are comfortable navigating its lower-level API.

For Laravel projects specifically, packages that wrap these underlying engines can simplify the integration, allowing you to handle template loading and data injection without managing the raw library calls yourself.
